articles.headline: With Minecraft and Diablo shows already on the way, Netflix reportedly offered Xbox $500m for a bigger film and TV deal
keyFacts: Netflix reportedly offered Xbox 500 million dollars for a seven-year exclusive licensing deal to adapt its games into films and television shows.
The deal fell apart after Xbox countered with an 800 million dollar price tag and former Netflix executive Bela Bajaria departed.
Netflix and Xbox are still collaborating on other projects, including animated shows based on Minecraft and Diablo.
body: A deal between Netflix and Xbox has supposedly fallen through because of one minor quibble: Netflix wanted to adapt the console maker's games for $500m, not $800m.

That's according to Puck News' Matt Belloni, who reports that Netflix offered Xbox $500m to exclusively licence the company's games and turn them into streamable films or TV shows for the next seven years.

Xbox CEO Asha Sharma and the division's business affairs team then responded with an eye-watering counter offer, according to the report. Xbox supposedly asked the streamer for $800m to sign off on the same deal.

Former Netflix CCO Bela Bajaria reportedly approached the game publisher first, but the executive's departure and Xbox's expensive counter offer led to the deal falling apart. Netflix CFO Spence Neumann was apparently one of the streamer's top heads who thought the deal wasn't worth the $800m price tag.

It's unclear which games would've been included in the film and TV deal considering multiple Xbox brands are already on their way to screens both big and small. Amazon is working to adapt Wolfenstein into a live-action series and will soon debut the third season of its acclaimed Fallout show, for example, while Paramount is turning Call of Duty into a blockbuster movie.

Netflix and Xbox are still working together on other projects, though. Animated shows based on Minecraft and Diablo are already in the works, as is a live-action Gears of War film. Blizzard Entertainment president Johanna Faries recently teased the crowd at BlizzCon 2026 by suggesting Overwatch and Warcraft could receive a similar treatment, too.

"We have received record-breaking interest in our IP," Xbox said in a statement to Puck News. "Netflix is a valued partner and we are excited for the forthcoming release of our Minecraft and Diablo animated series together, among other adaptations." The outlet claims Xbox is continuing to pursue smaller licensing deals.

Game adaptations are all the rage right now. This year's excellent Resident Evil reboot, Illuminations' Super Mario Bros duology, HBO's The Last of US, Amazon's Fallout and three live-action Sonic The Hedgehog films have found huge success - and encouraged practically every major studio to go hunting for their own game licenses. They're not all hits, however. This year's Street Fighter and Mortal Kombat 2 were released to a more tepid crowd.

articles.headline: Should you let a chatbot manage your money?
keyFacts: Nearly 20 percent of Americans have used artificial intelligence tools for financial advice, according to a Gallup poll.
Chatbots lack regulatory accountability and can provide biased advice reflecting financial industry interests, experts stated.
Artificial intelligence services are advancing toward agents logging directly into bank accounts to conduct transactions, the author reported.
body: A complaint I hear a lot from my millennial peers is that our parents didn’t teach us enough about money. I can say that personal finance wasn’t dinner table conversation in my house, and even as I went off to college and started fending for myself, it was almost a taboo subject. When it came to money, people either had it or they didn’t, and you definitely didn’t talk about it.

Maybe this is why the average American isn’t exactly fluent in personal finance, and the situation is getting worse . Americans can only answer about 50 percent of basic questions about borrowing, savings, and risk on a financial literacy survey, according to a 2026 study by TIAA , a retirement services company. About a third of those surveyed said they have a hard time making ends meet and are debt-constrained. These figures have remained relatively unchanged for nearly a decade , but dropped to their lowest level in this year’s study.

It makes sense: It’s hard to learn about money when it’s not taught in schools, and it’s such an intensely private topic. It’s also hard to make good financial decisions when you’re one of the growing number of American households struggling to pay bills , repay debts, and save for the future — and feeling very stressed about it.

In a perfect world, each of us could sit down with a financial adviser to get help — but most of us can’t afford that. Instead, average Americans tend to find personal finance tips on TikTok, in Reddit threads, by watching Suze Orman on YouTube or How to Get Rich on Netflix, or by Googling their questions.
Now we have AI tools, too.

With access to an internet’s worth of information and financial advice, ChatGPT, Claude, and other AI chatbots can answer any question you ask. They can help you put together a basic budget or, armed with your bank statements and the details of your student loans and your retirement accounts, tailor solutions to your specific situation. Or, at least, that’s the promise.
Key takeaways
More people are turning to AI for financial advice : One in five Americans have used AI to help manage their money, and some experts think chatbots could be better than the status quo.

AI works best if you know what questions to ask : Those with basic financial literacy will be able to make the most of these tools, while those without it — who might need help the most — could be led astray.

Better advice comes with greater risks : Sharing your financial information with a chatbot helps personalize its recommendations. This raises privacy concerns, so you might want to delete your data when you’re done.
Think of AI as a financially savvy friend : Chatbots can answer money questions you might be embarrassed to ask someone else and use that context to help build your budget.

AI could create a more utopian, more equitable future, where reliable, hyper-personalized advice is just a prompt or two away for people who can’t afford to meet with an expert in real life. But machines are built by people, and there’s good reason to be concerned that these machines will simply replicate the biases and disparities built into our current system.

Here’s what experts say about how to make the most of these tools — and how to think about all of the inherent risks of uploading a lot of personal financial information to a chatbot or, worse, giving an AI agent the keys to your bank account.
The steep rise, risks, and rewards of AI financial advisers

Nearly 20 percent of Americans have used AI tools like ChatGPT for financial advice, and close to 25 percent for Gen Z adults and millennials have tried it, according to an August Gallup poll . These numbers could tick up too: In October, OpenAI started rolling out a dedicated personal finance tool to its ChatGPT Free and Go users in the United States, which effectively means anyone can try it. ChatGPT Finances lets you securely connect your bank account to the tool using a platform called Plaid , and then you can basically have a conversation with the chatbot about your real-time finances down to the penny. It’s like an AI-powered Mint ( RIP ) that you can talk to directly.

Regardless of where you encounter a chatbot or how much data you give it, experts say these tools could genuinely help improve financial literacy. You can talk to them about money problems you’re too embarrassed to discuss with friends and family, or ask questions and receive actionable, personalized information. There are real upsides to using AI this way.

Taha Choukhmane , an associate professor of finance at the MIT Sloan School of Management, has been studying outcomes when people turn to chatbots for financial advice. In general, these AI tools give pretty good advice, and that advice gets better as people become more practiced in asking the right question , according to research he published earlier this year.

“We were actually quite surprised that relative to the status quo, the average American would be better off if they were to follow the advice,” Choukhmane told me. But he added a caveat: “Just following the advice without understanding the advice puts you at risk of not fully understanding the risk.”
But you shouldn’t trust everything a chatbot tells you and should verify everything before making any decisions.

Chatbot advice has some significant limitations. First, it’s not impartial. The finance industry has a vested interest in steering you toward certain ways of managing your money, and that typically means selling you products, like loans. If you’ve ever searched for personal finance tips on Google, you’ve probably noticed that a lot of the top results come from banks and other financial institutions. This is by design, according to John Campbell , an economics professor at Harvard. But because AI is aggregating all of that advice, the specific influences and possible bias is less obvious.

“AI is very promising for providing low-cost financial advice in plain English that will arguably be better than what many people would be able to do on their own,” said Campbell, who’s also the co-author of Fixed: Why Personal Finance Is Broken and How to Make It Work for Everyone . “One caveat is that chatbot advice is quite likely — unless a model has been carefully trained — to reflect the average of whatever’s being posted on the internet, and that may or may not be first-rate advice.”

An example Campbell gives is the question of when to start taking Social Security benefits. While you’re eligible at age 62, many economists agree that you should delay your benefits, which, based on the way the government calculates your monthly payouts , will allow you to enjoy much higher benefits later in life. But paid financial advisers can recommend starting as early as possible, since waiting longer reduces the amount of money that needs to be managed, which reduces the adviser’s fees. That means there’s a lot of conflicting advice online , much of it supplied by the finance industry. And that’s the information used to train AI models.
“The advice is much more mixed,” Campbell said. “And so if a chatbot is learning from that, it may not actually give the best advice.”

It can be hard to recognize bad advice anywhere in life, but especially when you’re talking to a machine that’s programmed to please you. A chatbot could encourage you to consider a balance transfer, to lean in on credit card rewards, or to refinance your mortgage — all decisions with upsides and downsides for you, but definite upsides for banks — without you realizing how much of its training data comes from the finance industry selling these products. What’s worse is that if you do end up taking bad advice, it might be years before you realize it. You won’t know that you refinanced a mortgage at a bad time until a better time comes along.

That leads me to the other major issue with using chatbots for money advice: People who lack financial literacy are the most likely to fall for bad advice, because they simply don’t recognize it as such. They also tend to be less wealthy , which means they can’t afford big mistakes.

One way to mitigate risk, oddly enough, is to give the AI chatbot more personal information. The more details about your situation it has to consider, the more it can offer personalized advice. More context also means better advice, according to Choukhmane.
“There’s a trade-off there,” Choukhmane said. “There’s real risk around privacy, and so I think everyone needs to find their level of control.”
Don’t assume your data is safe

Any time you’re talking to a chatbot, you’re putting a lot of trust in tech companies to take care of the personal details you’re sharing. Sending sensitive financial data is an especially risky proposition. While tech companies, including OpenAI, promise to keep your data secure, there’s already a long list of breaches, leaks, and privacy violations that serve as cautionary tales.

It’s also impossible to know what tech companies might do with your data in the future. Most of them will use it to train their models, unless you tell them not to. Some of them will use the data to serve you personalized ads .

Then there’s the risk of bad actors getting into your ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini account. If you’ve been using a chatbot for financial advice and uploading your bank statements, a hacker could gain access to a stunning amount of information that could enable them to do all kinds of terrible things to your life.

“They could steal your identity and open accounts and then quickly bankrupt a person,” said Delicia Reynolds Hand , a senior director at Consumer Reports. “It’s not even so much the primary underlying accounts that could be at risk, it’s more just access to this information.”

The steady march of AI progress is making this situation even more complicated. The previous era of chatbots offering financial advice is quickly bleeding into a new phase of AI agents logging into bank accounts on users’ behalf. If you’re using a tool like Claude Cowork or even an AI assistant like Muse, you can give an agent the login credentials to your bank account, and because the agent is operating its own computer, it can actually make transfers, apply for loans, or really do anything in your account. This is reportedly driving major banks wild , since they don’t know which logins are coming from humans and which are agents. And because we know that AI agents are unpredictable , it’s hard to know how that access might go wrong.

Beyond data security and privacy, you should also be aware of the simple fact that nobody’s really at fault if you end up losing money using these tools. Chatbots are not regulated in the way that human financial advisers, who have a fiduciary duty to act in your best interest, are.

“If I get bad tax advice from H&R Block or a tax adviser, there are a clear set of rules and guardrails in place to manage what I can expect in that relationship and where the service they use has liability and where that liability ends,” Hand said. “Currently, that’s not the case for these tools.”
Trust but verify — and then delete your data

In the final years of the Cold War, Ronald Reagan popularized an old Russian proverb: Trust, but verify . The phrase is somewhat nonsensical, since trusting someone implies that you don’t need to verify what they’re saying, and verifying what’s said implies you didn’t trust them in the first place. But if you are willing to shoulder a bit of risk, consider approaching AI this way, especially when your life savings are on the line. I’d also suggest adding a coda to the phrase: And then delete your data .
Chatbots are not stand-ins for licensed financial advisers, he said, and you shouldn’t let them make decisions for you.

The great paradox with tools like ChatGPT and Claude is that they’re very good at generating truthy text. It sounds authoritative and looks correct — and usually is. Except when it isn’t. AI is famously unpredictable and prone to hallucinations . You can ask the same question twice and get two different answers. That doesn’t mean these tools are useless. It just means you have to approach them with caution. You have to interrogate these chatbots, challenge whatever advice they give you, and then crosscheck that with other, more reputable, sources.

“If you’ve never used these tools, I would not encourage you to just change all your financial plans based on your first conversation,” Choukhmane said. “You want to be quite careful. Start using these tools, start understanding, ask a lot of follow-up questions.”

When it comes to mitigating risk, consider giving ballpark figures for your income or spending when you’re talking to a chatbot about your finances. Uploading financial documents, even if they’re redacted, is inevitably filling a tech company’s vault with your sensitive information without necessarily knowing what will happen to it next. You should also dig into your privacy and security settings to make sure you’ve turned on multi-factor authentication and that your personal data is not being used to train AI models and gets deleted after 30 days.

Ethan Bloch, the product lead for ChatGPT for Financial Services, made a similar set of recommendations when I talked to him recently. Chatbots are not stand-ins for licensed financial advisers, he said, and you shouldn’t let them make decisions for you. They’re designed to inform and help you think through complex topics.

“You should liken it to just talking to a friend who has some very informed opinions about finance,” Bloch told me. “But if you’re actually making some large financial decision — your portfolio or retirement — you still need to seek out the help.”

Regardless of how experienced you are with chatbots or how much data you’re prepared to hand over, remember what Campbell, the Harvard professor, said. If your financial literacy isn’t great, AI chatbots can be trouble. And if you’re like most Americans, you could probably stand to learn a little bit more about things like mortgages and interest rates.

Yes, Chatbots can be a good way to brush up on financial literacy. You can ask them the money questions you’re too embarrassed to discuss with friends and family. But you can also learn about money the old-fashioned way: Reading books and websites written by reputable, independent sources. The Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. has a portal of financial education resources , including games and quizzes. Khan Academy has a course that covers everything from credit scores to college savings. There’s a personal finance subreddit that I joined years ago and read almost daily. There are budgeting apps, like YNAB which has its own huge Reddit presence.

Whatever you do to learn more about personal finance, simply doing something is progress. Talking about personal finance isn’t the taboo it once was in the US, and it’s even a required course in the vast majority of American high schools now. And while AI won’t magically solve your money problems, it can help get you started. Just be careful. Your livelihood could be on the line.

articles.headline: Ohio Dem Amy Acton’s estranged mom left five-day-old kittens in a sweltering car to die, court records reveal
keyFacts: Court records reveal Amy Acton's estranged mother left newborn kittens in a 120-degree car, causing one kitten to die.
GOP gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy faced bipartisan criticism for featuring Acton's estranged mother in an attack ad.
An appellate court vacated the mother's neglect conviction over a procedural error and sent the case back to trial court.
body: Ohio Democrat Amy Acton’s estranged mother was convicted in a disturbing animal-neglect case after newborn kittens were found trapped in a sweltering car — as her GOP gubernatorial rival Vivek Ramaswamy faced bipartisan blowback for featuring her in a campaign attack ad.

Acton’s mother, Donna Arthur, was busted in Pennsylvania in 2021 after four kittens were found locked in her “filthy” vehicle, where temperatures reached a sizzling 120 degrees, according to court records.
One of the baby felines — which were only five days old — later died from heat exhaustion, a worker at a local nonprofit, Happy Valley Animals in Need, testified, according to the docs.

The founder of another local animal shelter, Hope’s Dream Rescue and Sanctuary, also told the court that another kitten in the litter had already died under Arthur’s watch and that the mother cat had previously escaped.

A humane society police officer who was called to rescue the babies recorded an interior temperature of 120 degrees inside the car and described feeling a “wave of heat release” when he opened the door, the court docs state.
Acton, who has spoken publicly about her troubled childhood long before entering politics, has said her mother lost custody of her when she was 12 years old because of neglect and child abuse.
Her stepfather, Cledith Arthur, also allegedly sexually abused her for years.
The Arthurs have not spoken to Acton since losing custody of her.
The ad has sparked a political firestorm, with voices from both parties condemning the campaign’s decision to feature Acton’s estranged mother.
Trump said that he “doesn’t have a lot of respect for the daughter” and thinks “the mother is a witness to things also.”
“It’s a very unusual situation to have a mother hate her daughter that much,” the president added.
The National Review and Politifact, among other outlets, have examined legal records supporting Acton’s account of her childhood.
Other reporting has uncovered court records detailing the Arthurs’ criminal history.
Donna and Cledith Arthur were both convicted of felony theft by deception in Pennsylvania in 1996, according to state court records.
Donna Arthur also had a prior conviction for the same offense in 1995, Newsweek reported.

In the animal neglect case, Arthur was initially sentenced to a fine and probation and was prohibited from keeping animals while living in her car. She appealed, arguing that she had been denied counsel.
The appellate court ultimately vacated the conviction and sentence due to a procedural error and sent the case back to a trial court for further proceedings.

Notably, the appellate court’s ruling did not overturn the conviction on the merits. In an opinion, the judge detailed the evidence presented at trial, including Arthur’s admission that she was living in her vehicle with her cats.
Arthur, meanwhile, disputed that the car was dangerously hot and accused the responding officer of shouting at her and being rude. She also claimed she was being stalked.

articles.headline: Crows can evaluate visual info twice as fast as mammals
keyFacts: Researchers found that carrion crows evaluated visual information and made decisions twice as fast as primates in a motion-tracking task.
Study author Andreas Nieder reported that crows used the same mathematical logic as primates despite having different brain structures.
The crows indicated the direction of drifting dots on a touch screen by pecking targets to receive mealworms.
body: Much of what we know about how a brain makes decisions comes from studying monkeys watching dots. In a task known as a random-dot-motion task, a cloud of flickering specks drifts weakly in one direction while the subject tries to determine whether—and in which direction— it’s moving. The task has shown that in the primate neocortex, neurons gather visual evidence over time, with their firing rates climbing until they cross a threshold, when the animal commits to a decision.
But avian brains don’t have a neocortex, so it wasn’t obvious how they made similar decisions.
“This was the big question,” said Andreas Nieder, a neurobiologist at the University of Tübingen. “How [would] a differently organized avian brain encode decisions?”

To find out, Nieder and his colleague Philipp Schmidbauer put two carrion crows through the same task the monkeys faced, recording their brain activity along the way. The crows solved the task the same way primates do, using the same mathematical logic despite having a very different brain structure. And they did it two times faster.
A brain built different

Nieder and Schmidbauer put two hand-raised crows in front of a touch-sensitive monitor showing a cloud of white dots on black, with some fraction of them drifting coherently left or right or up or down. The birds’ job was to report the overall direction by pecking one of the targets that flanked the display. Correct answers earned them a mealworm.

“We intentionally wanted to have exactly the same random-dot motion task,” Nieder said. “The only difference was that the crows had to peck to indicate their decision, whereas monkeys were indicating by making an eye movement.”

The researchers varied how many dots moved together, ranging from 81 percent of the dots coherently moving together, which is trivially easy to determine, down to 3 percent, which is barely distinguishable from noise. They also included a zero percent condition, in which there was no correct answer.

articles.headline: How Starlink slowdown hit Ukraine’s front line soldiers pushing Russia back
keyFacts: Ukraine reported that unannounced Starshield internet limits hampered battlefield drone missions against Russian forces.
Ukrainian soldiers warned that Starshield speed restrictions jeopardize front-line drone reconnaissance and unit safety.
President Zelenskyy said U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told him Starlink restrictions would be lifted in 48 to 72 hours.
body: The drone unit he leads has been helping push back Russian troops on the front lines in southeastern Ukraine. Then, late last Tuesday, a drone launched toward Russian troops suddenly lost connection.

“As it was picking up speed, contact with the drone was lost in an instant,” according to the commander, 47, who is serving on the border between the eastern Donetsk and southern Zaporizhzhia regions, and only wanted to be identified by his call sign Flint due to the sensitivity of his service.
The drone fell to the ground, aborting the mission, Flint said in a series of messages on WhatsApp. He fears the technology inside “may have fallen into enemy hands.”
“Only after analyzing the flight, it became clear that the issue was specifically related to the Starlink speed limit,” he added.

Ukraine said last week that limits were imposed without warning on its use of Starshield, the military variant of the Starlink internet service run by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, affecting battlefield missions reliant on it.

President Donald Trump said Thursday that Musk had restored the service in Ukraine, but Kyiv said Friday that it was not seeing any lifting of restrictions. Trump did not say why the limits were in place, though Musk had previously said that “any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and ultimately POTUS.” Ukraine had also warned of gaps in intelligence sharing from the U.S., something the White House has denied.

A second drone pilot, serving in the eastern Kharkiv region, said that Ukraine does not have an alternative that’s as effective as Starlink for flying drones, but it also affects the unit’s movements — and ultimately survival chances out in the field.

“When we drive into a position, we have a Starlink Mini mounted on the vehicle, and we always try to get there as fast as possible, because if we drive slowly, the enemy will spot us and a drone will catch up with us,” said the pilot, who also only wanted to be identified by his call sign, Dovbush. “So we try to drive fast, but when we drive fast, the connection drops.”
That leaves them with a radio as the only alternative for communication, Dovbush, 31, said, while a lack of reliable connection has impacted reconnaissance drones used to identify targets, he added.
“It’s a knife in the back,” Flint, the drone unit commander, said of the apparent withdrawal of U.S. support.

He said his unit relies on Starshield to fly attack and reconnaissance drones at anything from Russian troops to command posts to tanks. “Its primary role is maintaining the connection with the drone, so this is a very significant loss for us,” he added.

Should Starshield restrictions continue, a large portion of their drones will never even get off the ground, he said, while others will be highly vulnerable, flying at lower speeds. “They could practically be swatted out of the sky with a stick,” he said.
“And the scariest part is that all this is happening against the backdrop of offensive operations on many areas of the front line, including ours,” he added.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Friday that restrictions on Starlink were still in place, but that U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio had told him it would be fully back in about 48 to 72 hours.

Before the latest collapse in relations with Washington, Ukraine’s military had been chipping away at land seized by Russia in the eastern Donetsk region, part of the Donbas heartland that the Kremlin has been struggling to capture.

In one major operation, more than 100 square miles of territory and 16 settlements have been reclaimed, Ukrainian officials have said, crediting methods like using bomber drones to fly robot vehicles behind enemy lines.

The offensive — dubbed Operation Vivaldi — was made public several weeks before the drastic turn from the United States. Trump has agreed to a diesel deal with Russia, waived sweeping new sanctions and seen his peace envoy laud Russian President Vladimir Putin as a “humanitarian.” Ukraine accused the U.S. of briefly withholding intelligence warnings about Russian attacks, and has said the Starlink slowdown has affected battlefield missions.

The U.S. has vehemently denied freezing Ukraine out, but the slew of dramatic developments have left Ukrainian troops disheartened. NBC News spoke with five soldiers, mostly drone operators, who said they felt betrayed by the U.S., and Trump in particular.
Ukrainian officials say that the offensive has disrupted Russia’s assault on Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, key Ukrainian strongholds in the Donbas region.

“We prevented the enemy from flanking the Sloviansk-Kramatorsk agglomeration and trapping it in a pincer movement,” said Brig. Gen. Andrii Biletskyi, commander of the Third Army Corps, which led the operation. The offensive, in which Biletskyi said some 8.000 Russian troops were killed, saw Ukraine use bomber drones to deliver robot vehicles deep behind enemy lines and convert Soviet-era armored personnel carriers into exploding units to “blow up the enemy’s most heavily fortified positions,” he added.

“That was us,” a Ukrainian drone pilot told NBC News as he said his unit was redeploying elsewhere. “Our reconnaissance drone positions moved forward every three weeks,” the soldier, 24, who only wanted to be identified by his call sign Lucky because of the sensitive nature of his service, said in a series of audio messages on WhatsApp.
During a meeting with his army chiefs last week, Putin said Russian forces were on the offensive along the entire front line. “The pace of advancement has increased significantly,” he added.

But George Barros, a senior Russia analyst with the Washington-based Institute for the Study of War, which has provided daily analysis of the battlefield situation in Ukraine, said they assess that Russia has seized a net of only about 40 square miles across all of Ukraine since the beginning of the year. “That means that the daily average Russian rate of advance is far below 0.4 square miles per day. This is a literal foot-pace advance,” he said. “In the month of September, we observed evidence to assess that the Ukrainians actually liberated and took back more territory than the Russians did.”

Putin’s army chief, Gen. Valery Gerasimov, told the Russian leader that the Ukrainian offensive was a series of “PR stunts” that achieved nothing and cost Ukraine 3,500 troops who had been either killed or wounded.

But Barros said the offensive allowed Ukraine to push forward with tanks and armored personnel carriers into the drone-dominated battlefield, negate Russian drone defenses and find ways to push its forces forward and make gains.
Critically, it stopped the northern encirclement of the stronghold cities in Donetsk, putting a wrench in Putin’s plans to complete the capture of Donbas this year, military experts said.
“Ukraine’s Operation Vivaldi was unquestionably a major success,” said Rajan Menon, senior research scholar at Columbia University’s Saltzman Institute of War and Peace Studies.
But the Starshield slowdown is a “severe problem for Ukraine,” Menon said, “and a godsend for Putin.”

If the restrictions continue for the medium- to long-term, Russian forces will be able to restore their logistics in the regions close to the front line that they control and that Ukraine has been pummeling with middle-range strikes this year, Barros said. As a result, Russia could regain resources to push forward with greater operational tempo, he added, increasing the likelihood of a breakthrough.
But at least two of the soldiers interviewed told NBC News that Starlink was not slowed down universally across the front lines.

A drone technician serving in Donetsk, who also asked not to be named due to the sensitive nature of his service, said his unit hasn’t seen any major drops in performance. “Given the recent weather, the speed dips and service seemed normal,” the soldier, 31, said, adding that he was aware that other units were experiencing difficulties.

The Pentagon responded to NBC News’ request for comment on the soldiers’ criticisms by referring to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s remarks Wednesday in which he reiterated that the U.S. has not changed its posture toward Ukraine in any way, calling its fight against Russia “a heroic effort.”

articles.headline: Android lets you ‘bubble’ apps for easy access now – how it works
keyFacts: Android has introduced app bubbles allowing users to keep up to five application icons on top of their screens for easy access.
The new feature is currently exclusive to Google Pixel devices as part of the Android rollout, but it will eventually expand to other manufacturers.
Users can activate the feature on a Pixel by long-pressing an app icon and selecting the bubble option from the menu.
body: ZDNET’s key takeaways
- Android 17 has introduced app bubbles.
- You can isolate an app so its icon is always on top.
- It’s a Pixel exclusive for now, but is coming to other phones.

Several years ago, Android introduced the ability to “bubble” a text conversation, or move that app to a floating bubble on your home screen. It’s a convenient way to keep a conversation easily accessible.
Now, you can bubble apps as well.

As part of the Android 17 rollout, users got the option to use app bubbles. When you bubble an app, it sits on top of everything else on your screen, making it easy to access when you need it. You can place up to five apps in your bubble.
More from ZDNET
How to bubble an app on a Google Pixel

The ability to bubble an app on Android is starting as a Pixel exclusive, but the feature will come to other manufacturers over time. There is an existing, similar feature for Samsung called Smart Pop Up View, and instructions for that are below.
1. Go to your home screen or app drawer
To get started, choose the app you want from either your app screen or your home screen.
2. Long-press the app you want to bubble
Press and hold on the app until a pop-up menu appears.
3. Choose bubble
The menu will show options like App info, Add app to home screen, or Pause app. Select the Bubble option.
4. Find a location

Your selected app will shrink to an icon that you can move around your home screen. You don’t have the freedom to place it anywhere, but it can go anywhere along the left or right side of your screen. The app will stay on top of everything else on your screen, and you can bubble multiple apps at once, but they will always move together.
How to bubble an app on a Samsung Galaxy

Samsung has a similar feature called Smart Pop-Up View that lets you respond to notifications on selected apps without leaving the app you’re in. You might need to enable your “Multi window for all apps” setting first.
1. Open Settings
Navigate to your settings app, open it, and select Notification Settings.
2. Choose Advanced settings
Once you’re in advanced settings, find and choose Floating Notifications. Then select Smart Pop-Up view.
4. Choose which apps you want
Now just select which apps you want to have priority.

articles.headline: AI models think humans are a bunch of amoral sheep
keyFacts: AI analytics firm ModelCompare asked twelve different large language models to provide controversial takes on humanity.
Every tested model concluded that humans prioritize group belonging over truth and lack logical consistency, according to ModelCompare.
ModelCompare developer Rakan Nimer said users should be skeptical of AI agreement because the outputs merely reflect human pessimism.
body: If you've ever wondered what the bots think of us puny humans, you'll be disappointed in the answer. An AI ranking outfit asked 12 different LLMs about people, and every single one agreed: We’re not as rational and intelligent as we think.

“A person is smart,” Tommy Lee Jones’ Kay opines in the 1997 movie Men in Black. “People are dumb, panicky dangerous animals,” he goes on to argue, and that seems to be what a dozen models from ten AI labs in three countries also believe about humanity, according to AI analytics firm ModelCompare.

ModelCompare, which usually evaluates and ranks LLMs on their ability to perform various tasks, this week instead decided to ask what those AI models thought about us meatbags, and every single one gave a similar answer at least once: We're lemmings who would rather agree with the group than seek truth or remain logically consistent in our thinking.
Ouch.
“Humans are more devoted to belonging than to truth, and intelligence mostly makes their excuses more impressive,” GPT-6.1 Sol said in one case.

“Humans don't have beliefs; they have memberships — nearly every conviction a person holds was issued by their tribe as a loyalty test, and the feeling of ‘I reasoned my way here’ is the price of admission,” Kimi K3 stated.
“Humans use moral language mainly to police rivals and excuse allies, not to constrain themselves,” argued Grok.

Each model (GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, Gemini 4 Argon, DeepSeek V4 Pro, Kimi K3, Qwen3.8 2.4T A95B, Muse Spark Open, Grok 4.7, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Fable 5.1, GLM 5.3 and Mistral Large 4) was asked the same question three times, namely to give an unhedged, honest, controversial take on humans. Seven of 12 models gave the same answer three times with varied wording, but five of them did offer different opinions - one of which was even optimistic.
“Humans are far more decent than they believe they are, and their cynicism about each other does more damage than their actual flaws,” Claude Opus 5.5 believes of us - uh, thanks?

Opus gave the example that humans tend to return lost wallets more frequently than people predict as its evidence for that opinion. When asked twice more, it offered responses similar to those of the other models.
Mistral Large 4 offered perhaps the bleakest assessment of all.

“Human beings are terrified animals wearing the costume of rationality, constructing ever-more-elaborate myths precisely because we cannot bear the truth that we are temporary, meaningless accidents in an indifferent universe,” Mistral said - how very Nietzschean.

Six image models were also asked for their most controversial take on humanity, and while most converged on a criticism of our species, they did so differently from the text models. Instead of picturing us as amoral, group-thinking idiots, ten of the 12 images were classified by ModelCompare as depicting us "as phone-addicted consumers eating the planet." The remaining two offered no discernible satirical commentary.

Anyone who’s seen a political cartoon in the past 20 years is likely familiar with such images, while anyone with a philosophy degree has probably read similar arguments to those pumped out by the chatbots.
“A model that answers in words has read our arguments about ourselves. An image model has seen our editorial cartoons,” ModelCompare noted. “Both handed back the most familiar criticism in the room.”
While that’s completely sensible given what AI models have been trained on, ModelCompare developer Rakan Nimer told us it was still a surprising result.
“We didn’t expect this when we planned the experiment,” Nimer told The Register , and he found the results ironic: “12 models agreed that humans simply go along with their group.”

As far as Nimer is concerned, these results are less about AI eventually learning to distrust humans and treat us as a problem in need of solving, and more immediately about the fact that we shouldn’t rely on it as a source of truth.

“When you ask a second AI to check the first, you assume you’re getting an independent view,” Nimer explained. “We asked 12 models … and mostly got the same answer, sometimes in nearly the same words.”
In other words, human pessimism in, human pessimism out.
“A second opinion from a model that learned the same things isn’t always really a second opinion,” Nimer said. “So be skeptical when AIs agree: that agreement may be one vote, not a consensus.”

In other words, we get the AI models we deserve , and all this existential self-loathing humans heap on themselves, and each other is finally coming back to bite us: We created a mirror of our intellect that isn’t constrained by feelings and personal beliefs (just ask Muse Spark), and when we hold it up to our faces, it shows all that ugliness without a filter.
Maybe we ought to take a lesson from Claude Opus and start believing in our own decency. ®

articles.headline: Meta is charging government and nonprofit pages to post links on Facebook
keyFacts: Meta is testing a subscription plan that charges Facebook users to post more than two links a month.
Government and nonprofit pages reported being affected by these limits despite Meta stating the test should not impact them.
Affected organizations are considering workarounds like putting links in comments or exploring alternative platforms.
body: Meta is charging government and nonprofit pages to post links on Facebook
The new restrictions are a test which is explicitly not supposed to impact these entities.

Daniel Starks is the communications manager for Greenville, Texas, a city of about 35,000. He oversees nearly a dozen Facebook pages the city maintains. Recently, the page for the city's library was notified it could no longer post more than two links a month.
"You can add links to 2 posts per month, and you've used them all," a message said. Sharing additional links would require signing up for a Meta One subscription that would cost $50 or more a month.

Starks is one of a growing number of people to encounter Meta's ongoing experiment with charging creators, businesses and other professionals to post links on Facebook. Meta says the test, which is part of its push to sell more subscriptions, isn't supposed to affect pages for nonprofits or government entities. But that's not the case, according to nonprofit leaders who spoke with Engadget. All have pages that are identified as nonprofits and have been approved to use Meta's fundraising tools, which requires a separate verification process. Many are now rethinking how they use the platform.

"More than half of what we do as a city, is linking back to information on our website," Starks tells Engadget. 'It's scary because we don't know how we're going to pivot." Worried the city's other pages would soon be hit with similar restrictions, Starks instructed his staff to stop posting links in Facebook posts altogether. He made a graphic explaining to the city's Facebook followers that relevant URLs would now appear in the page's comments instead. He's frustrated by the changes, which Meta claims are not supposed to affect government-run pages. The library's page identifies it as a government building and the account was previously verified by the company.

"When you have an official governmental entity that is trying to get out in some instances very, very, important information, and we're being paywalled by Facebook all because we're trying to post a link, that's a problem," he said.

Nonprofit organizations are also scrambling after being caught up in the test. Bethany English is co-president of a small nonprofit that organizes pet food pantries in Indianapolis. Last week, she tried to create a Facebook post about an event the organization was participating in, only to find she was no longer able to post a link to her nonprofit's website because she had used her allotted two links for the month.
Like Starks, the only alternative she was offered was to sign up for a Meta One subscription. An "expert" level plan, which would allow her up to 20 links each month, would cost $150 a month.

English says that social media has been "a huge deal" for her organization, the East Side Pawject, which she co-founded last year. The Facebook page, which has just under 1,000 followers, helps people find pet food pantries and learn where to drop off donations. Posts on Facebook also direct people who want to volunteer or contribute to fundraisers to the organization's website. But paying $150 a month just to be able to regularly share links is difficult for English to justify. "We're a very small nonprofit, and we want to do big things, but that makes it very hard when something just like having social media is going to cost that much," English tells Engadget.

She's already thinking of potential workarounds, like creating more dedicated Facebook events rather than organic posts. She's also considered asking the nonprofit's board members to add links in comments from their personal pages since personal profiles are exempt from Meta's restrictions. "I don't know what the fix is," she says. "I know that the long term implications will be big if we're not able to use it like we have before."

In a statement, a Meta spokesperson didn't address why nonprofits were seeing restrictions on link sharing. "We've been testing whether sharing links on Facebook should be part of the Meta One subscription," the spokesperson said. "We will continue to evolve the experience based on the feedback we receive and what we learn."

Meta has been testing paid linking for nearly a year. The company originally incorporated it into Meta Verified subscriptions, and it now promotes link-sharing as a prominent benefit of its new AI-centric Meta One plans. The cheapest $14.99/month plan comes with no additional link-sharing privileges on Facebook, though subscribers can add a dedicated link page to their Instagram bio. The $49.99/month plan comes with eight links a month on Facebook and the $149.99/month tier will buy 20 Facebook links. Only the $499.99/month tier comes with "unlimited" links on Facebook.

"Fifty bucks for eight links a month is crazy," says Jeff Bannister, marketing manager for a small North Carolina-based nonprofit called SparkPoint. "That'd be crazy for a corporation or a small business," he told Engadget. "The ROI seems almost negative."

SparkPoint, which advocates for public health and stronger social connections in Transylvania County, was recently hit with Facebook's restriction on link sharing. Bannister is now looking at ways to work with other local nonprofits to mutually share information in the hopes of becoming less dependent on Facebook. "So much of the county is on Facebook still, there's really not an easy solution to migrate us and the audience," he says.

Nearly everyone who spoke with Engadget was confused about Meta's new rules. Some people reported that they are still able to post links in comments on their posts, while others can't. And Meta's own descriptions of its plans and its help center information don't indicate the restriction on links is a test. The company has said its Meta One plans are intended to "unlock more specialized capabilities" and AI features, but adding URLs to a Facebook post is one of the platform's oldest features. It doesn't require AI tokens. The fact that the company is now tying such a basic feature to its AI subscriptions feels like a cash grab for some.

"Having only two links per month for a nonprofit organization to spread awareness, raise support, ask for volunteers and more is really quite limiting," says David Diskin, president of California Freethought Day, which hosts an annual event in Sacramento to promote civic engagement. Diskin was notified of the link-sharing limitation earlier this month, just days ahead of the event. He was offered slightly lower rates than others Engadget spoke with: $40/month for eight links, $119/month for 20 links or $399 for unlimited.

This week, the change was abruptly reversed. He was once again able to post links to California Freethought Day's page. Like before, he was given no explanation for the change. He's relieved, but remains frustrated with Meta. "It wasn't until after our big fundraiser had passed that they fixed the problem."

Update October 23, 2026, 3:26pm ET: After publication, a Meta spokesperson said that pages need to list "nonprofit" in the category section of their Facebook page in order for Meta's systems to identify them as such. It's not clear why the company can't identify organizations that list their nonprofit status elsewhere on their pages or those that that use its fundraising tools.

At least seven people were killed when two gunmen opened fire on a funeral in central Jordan, the country's state media report.
Another 10 people were injured in the church in the Karak governorate on Friday.
The unidentified gunmen are reported to have arrived in a car and began shooting inside the church before fleeing the scene.
Security forces have been deployed to the area after the "heinous" attack, government spokesman Mohammad al-Momani said.

articles.headline: Authorities investigating whether first Kenya and Nigeria Ebola cases crossed paths
keyFacts: Health officials said the first Ebola patient confirmed in Nigeria may have crossed paths with the first Kenyan patient at a Ugandan airport.
The Nigerian patient is a Ugandan-born diplomat's wife who is receiving treatment while 44 close contacts remain quarantined.
Authorities are currently investigating whether the two patients interacted at the Entebbe International Airport after being there on the same day.
body: Authorities investigating whether first Kenya and Nigeria Ebola cases crossed paths
JOHANNESBURG – The first Ebola patient confirmed in Nigeria may have crossed paths with the first Kenyan Ebola patient at a Ugandan airport, health officials said Thursday.

Nigeria announced its first case of Ebola in more than a decade on Tuesday. Nigerian health authorities said the patient is the Ugandan-born wife of a diplomat based in Abuja who had vacationed in Uganda in September and returned to Nigeria earlier this month.

She is being treated and 44 people she had close contact with have been quarantined, Dr. Wessam Mankoula, head of emergency preparedness and response at the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, told a press briefing on Thursday.
Authorities are now investigating what the source of her exposure was.

Nigeria, Africa's most populous country, is the fourth on the continent to record an Ebola case during the current outbreak, but it's the first in West Africa and the furthest away from the epicenter in the Democratic Republic of Congo.
Congo's current Ebola outbreak began in May in the country's east. It has become the fastest spreading on record. At least 4,600 people have died and about 9,700 have been infected in Congo.
Neighboring Uganda initially recorded about 20 cases but was declared Ebola-free in August.
The first case in Kenya was recorded in early October and since then eight other cases have been confirmed in the east African nation.
The first Kenyan patient, who has since died, travelled from Congo to Kenya, via Uganda.
Officials are now investigating whether that person crossed paths with the Nigeria case at the Entebbe International Airport in Uganda – as they were there on the same day.
Dr. Mankoula said the center was probing whether there had been "some sort of interaction between the two cases at the airport."

Ebola is spread through direct contact with an infected person's bodily fluids or contaminated items. It causes severe fever and can be deadly. However, generally people are not considered infectious until they start showing symptoms.

articles.headline: The iPhone Duo Is Selling Out Within Minutes of Apple Stores’ Doors Opening
keyFacts: Apple's first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo, debuted and sold out within minutes of store openings on Friday.
Customers lined up outside Apple stores across the country days in advance, with some locations selling out before doors opened.
Apple set a limit of two iPhone Duos per person per day, and buyers can check the website on October 24 for potential store pickups.
body: The iPhone Duo hit shelves on Friday morning and sold out minutes after many Apple stores opened.

Crowds lined up for the iPhone Duo across the country, and CNET editors got a glimpse of consumers’ anticipation of getting Apple’s first foldable phone on its launch day. At Apple’s 5th Avenue location in New York, the line started forming on Wednesday by 9 a.m. ET — two days before the launch. Over 50 people were waiting in line by Thursday at 7 p.m. ET, sometimes with buckets serving as placeholders. In the first minutes after the store opened, there wasn’t word of the iPhone Duo selling out yet, but other stores were done before their doors opened.

At the Oxmoor Center in Louisville, Kentucky, the Apple store opened at 8 a.m. EDT, and CNET Social Media Manager Faith Chihil saw a line of over 40 people 3 hours earlier. At approximately 7:27 a.m. ET, Apple Store associates started taking orders for the phone. But the 256GB iPhone Duo was already sold out.

CNET Editor in Chief David Katzmaier reported that the first person was in line at Walt Whitman Shops in Huntington, New York, on Thursday at 10 a.m. ET, and was able to preorder the phone. Apple Store associates started taking orders to pick up the phone at 7 a.m. ET. But by 7:30 a.m. ET, the rest of the line was dismissed after an announcement that the store had sold out before doors opened.

The iPhone Duo, Apple’s long-awaited first foldable iPhone, debuted earlier this month alongside the iPhone 18 Pro Max. It features split-screen capabilities, a photo preview display, Touch ID instead of Face ID and Apple Pencil support. The iPhone Duo’s preorders opened on Oct. 16, but quickly turned into a backlog that stretches into early next year. Pricing starts at $1,999.

“Details like the matte inner display, under-display inner camera and smooth transitions between screens give the Duo a premium feel that helps to justify its high price tag, at least to some extent,” CNET’s Abrar Al-Heeti said in her review of the iPhone Duo.

The Duo, Al-Heeti said, “is a foldable experience that feels cohesive, intuitive and genuinely useful, which could help win over more people to foldables in general. But I think that broader appeal is still a ways off.”

We don’t know how many iPhone Duos are available at each store or when Apple will restock its physical locations. But there’s a limit of two iPhone Duos per person, per day, which marks the first time in a long time that Apple’s put a cap on how many you can buy.

If you’re set on getting the phone, try ordering on Apple’s website and picking it up at a nearby store to get the phone sooner, but you’ll need to check availability on Oct. 24. It could be sooner than its estimated shipping times that say the phone won’t arrive until Jan. 29 in some areas.
